meta.name: GetHired Interview Prep — Question Bank
meta.note: Static, role-gated interview prep content (V4-P5). No AI-generated or invented questions — every technical question and format note below is grounded in a Researcher subagent pass over real published sources (Indeed career advice, InfosecTrain, TryHackMe's blog, CyCognito, Web Asha, FinalRoundAI, Uninets, CyberTalents, WashU McKelvey Industry Connect) rather than general knowledge. `whatTheyreChecking` is this project's own framing of what the question is probing for, not a scripted answer — the point is orientation, not a script to memorize verbatim.
meta.sourcing_note: SOC Analyst questions sourced from Indeed India's SOC analyst interview guide and InfosecTrain's SOC analyst question list (both cite real recurring interview questions, including scenario-based alert-triage framing). VAPT questions sourced from CyCognito/Qualysec (VA-vs-PT distinction) and InfoSecWarrior's penetration-testing interview question compilation (OWASP Top 10, SQLi/XSS types, IDOR, testing types) plus Web Asha's VAPT interview guide (methodology stages, tool familiarity). Network Security Engineer questions sourced from FinalRoundAI's network security interview guide and Uninets' firewall interview question list. Behavioral questions sourced from CyberTalents' cybersecurity interview prep guide and WashU McKelvey Industry Connect's cybersecurity interview prep post. The STAR framework is confirmed standard, widely-taught interview advice (Indeed, The Muse, UW Careers), not invented for this project. Generalist deliberately samples a broad cross-section from all three specific tracks rather than going deep on one, matching how the master prompt frames Generalist as the broadest-view default track. Two things the research pass flagged but could not independently confirm as universal, so are described here as 'varies by employer' rather than stated as fact: whether VAPT interviews commonly include a take-home report-writing sample, and whether SOC interviews use one standardized live-SIEM-exercise format.
meta.readiness_note: A later pass added two things per technical question: `strongAnswerCovers` (the key points/structure a strong answer should hit — still not a scripted answer, just what a good one covers) and `testedIn` (a cross-link to the specific Assessment or Quiz category that objectively tests the same underlying skill). Interview Prep stays the content-review layer; the Assessment and Quiz remain the actual objective readiness signal — reading every question here still doesn't tell you if you could answer under pressure, so each question now points at where to genuinely test that, reusing the existing role-gated Assessment/Quiz categories rather than building a separate self-rating system. The STAR framework note also gained a worked mini-example (`workedExample`), since naming the acronym without showing what each part actually looks like in a real answer wasn't enough to use it.

roles.formatNote: SOC interviews increasingly lean scenario-based rather than pure definitions — expect to walk through a simulated alert or log excerpt out loud, sometimes in a SIEM tool (Splunk, QRadar, or an ELK stack), rather than just answering 'what is X'. Practicing with a free SIEM lab (Splunk's free trial, or Security Onion) before the interview is a commonly repeated piece of advice from SOC-focused sources. It also helps to be able to name the Cyber Kill Chain and MITRE ATT&CK as frameworks, even briefly — both come up as 'you should know these' references across SOC interview prep guides.

technicalQuestions.question: How would you react if you received an alert for a malware infection on an endpoint?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Whether you have an actual triage sequence in your head (isolate, confirm, scope, escalate) rather than jumping straight to 'wipe the machine' — process matters more than the specific tool names you use.
strongAnswerCovers: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network first, before deep investigation
Confirm the alert is real (not a false positive) using EDR/AV details
Scope the blast radius — what else did this host touch or access
Escalate per your team's severity/runbook once contained

technicalQuestions.question: How would you go about analyzing a suspected DDoS attack?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Whether you understand what a DDoS actually looks like in traffic data (volume spikes, source patterns) and can describe an escalation path, not just define the term.
strongAnswerCovers: Confirm the traffic spike against a normal baseline, not just a gut feeling
Identify the pattern — source IP diversity, targeted port/service, request type
Distinguish a genuine DDoS from a legitimate traffic spike (e.g. a marketing launch)
Escalate for mitigation (rate limiting, upstream scrubbing) once confirmed

technicalQuestions.question: If P1, P2, P3, and P4 incidents all came in around the same time, how would you decide what to work first?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Real prioritization judgment under pressure — this is one of the most repeated SOC interview questions because triage-under-load is the actual job.
strongAnswerCovers: A consistent framework for ranking (impact + urgency), not gut feel
Willingness to work multiple threads in parallel rather than strictly sequential
Communicating triage decisions to the team, not just making them silently

technicalQuestions.question: What's the difference between a HIDS and a NIDS, and when would you reach for each?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Whether you understand host-level visibility versus network-level visibility as genuinely different tools for different blind spots, not interchangeable acronyms.
strongAnswerCovers: HIDS watches a single host (file integrity, process activity); NIDS watches network traffic across many hosts
Each catches different blind spots — HIDS misses network-only attacks, NIDS misses encrypted or host-local activity
A mature SOC typically uses both together, not one instead of the other

technicalQuestions.question: What's a false positive, and would you rather a SIEM over-alert or under-alert?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Judgment, not a textbook definition — there's a real tradeoff between alert fatigue and missed detections, and the interviewer wants to see you reason about it.
strongAnswerCovers: Define a false positive clearly: an alert that looks malicious but isn't
Name the real tradeoff: too sensitive causes alert fatigue, too lenient misses real attacks
A reasoned position (e.g. lean toward over-alerting early, tune down over time) rather than a flat answer

technicalQuestions.question: Can you walk me through the steps of a TCP three-way handshake?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Baseline networking fluency — a huge share of SOC work is reading connection logs, and this checks whether that reading will make sense to you.
strongAnswerCovers: SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK, in that order
What each flag actually signals (connection request, acknowledgment plus own request, confirmation)
Why this matters for reading connection logs — e.g. spotting a scan when handshakes never complete

technicalQuestions.question: What is SIEM, and which SIEM tools (if any) have you used or practiced with?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Hands-on exposure over textbook knowledge — naming a tool you've actually clicked around in (even a free trial) lands better than reciting what SIEM stands for.
strongAnswerCovers: A real example of a SIEM or lab tool actually used (Splunk, ELK, Security Onion, etc.)
One concrete thing done in it — a query written, a dashboard read, an alert investigated
SIEM's core job in your own words: aggregating and correlating logs from many sources

technicalQuestions.question: Imagine 300 alerts fire at once. How would you figure out what to look at first?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Triage-at-scale reasoning — grouping duplicates, spotting a noisy misconfigured rule, and identifying genuine impact, not a memorized step order.
strongAnswerCovers: Group or deduplicate first — many alerts often trace back to one root cause or a noisy rule
Sort by real impact, not alert volume alone
Flag and suppress a clearly misconfigured rule rather than triaging it 300 times

roles.formatNote: VAPT interviewers commonly frame questions as scenarios ('you find X during a scan — what's your next step?') rather than pure definitions, and expect you to be able to walk through a full methodology end-to-end (recon → scanning → exploitation → reporting), not just list tool names. Some employers include a live or take-home practical exercise as part of the process, though this varies — don't assume there will or won't be one, and it's fine to ask what the interview format looks like when you're scheduling it.

technicalQuestions.question: What's the difference between a vulnerability assessment and a penetration test?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Whether you understand VA as broad, often automated detection versus PT as manual, goal-directed exploitation of real attack paths — this is one of the most commonly asked questions in the whole track.
strongAnswerCovers: VA: broad, often automated scanning for known vulnerabilities across many assets
PT: manual, goal-directed exploitation of real attack paths on a smaller scope
PT usually follows VA — VA finds candidates, PT proves which are actually exploitable

technicalQuestions.question: Walk me through the OWASP Top 10 categories you know best.
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Depth beyond a memorized list — can you explain why something like Broken Access Control or Injection is dangerous in your own words, with a concrete example.
strongAnswerCovers: Pick 2-3 categories you can explain in your own words, not recite
A concrete real-world example for each, not just the name
Why it's dangerous — the actual impact, not just the category label

technicalQuestions.question: Can you explain a few different types of SQL injection?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Whether you know the real variety (in-band/error-based, blind/inferential, out-of-band) rather than treating 'SQLi' as one flat thing.
strongAnswerCovers: In-band/error-based: the response directly shows the injected result or a DB error
Blind/inferential: no direct output, inferred via true/false or timing behavior
Out-of-band: relies on a separate channel (e.g. DNS) to exfiltrate results

technicalQuestions.question: What are the different types of XSS, and how would you mitigate them?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: The reflected/stored/DOM-based distinction plus real mitigations (output encoding, Content-Security-Policy) rather than a one-line 'sanitize input' answer.
strongAnswerCovers: Reflected: payload comes from the current request, executes immediately, isn't stored
Stored: payload saved server-side, executes for every later viewer
DOM-based: happens purely in client-side JS, never touches the server
Mitigation: output encoding plus a Content-Security-Policy, not just 'sanitize input'

technicalQuestions.question: What's an IDOR, and how would you go about testing for one?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Authorization-logic reasoning — IDOR is one of the most common real findings junior pentesters actually report, so this checks practical instinct, not trivia.
strongAnswerCovers: Definition: the app trusts an object reference (like an ID) from the client without checking ownership
How to test: change an ID you own to one you don't, in a request that should be scoped to you
Why it's common: it's an authorization bug, not a syntax bug, so scanners often miss it

technicalQuestions.question: What's the difference between black box, gray box, and white box testing?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Whether you understand how much information the tester starts with in each case, and how that changes your approach.
strongAnswerCovers: Black box: no internal knowledge, mirrors an external attacker
Gray box: some information (e.g. a user account), mirrors an insider or post-compromise scenario
White box: full access to source/config, focused on depth over realism

technicalQuestions.question: Walk me through your pentest methodology from start to finish.
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Structured thinking across the whole engagement (planning/recon → scanning → gaining access → maintaining access → analysis → reporting) — reporting counts as much as exploitation here.
strongAnswerCovers: Planning/scoping -> recon -> scanning -> exploitation -> post-exploitation -> reporting, in that order
Reporting counts as much as exploitation — a finding nobody can act on isn't useful
Respecting scope and rules of engagement throughout, not just at the start

technicalQuestions.question: Which tools have you actually used — Nmap, Burp Suite, Metasploit, Nessus, Nikto?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Real lab time over tool-name familiarity — be ready to describe one specific thing you did with a tool, not just that you've heard of it.
strongAnswerCovers: One specific thing actually done with each tool named, not just 'I've heard of it'
Nmap for recon/discovery, Burp for web app testing, Metasploit for exploitation, Nessus for vuln scanning
Comfort explaining why a tool fits a given step, not just its name

roles.formatNote: Expect OSI-model-anchored troubleshooting questions ('a device can't reach the internet — walk me through where you'd check') more than abstract theory. The interviewer is testing whether you can reason layer-by-layer under pressure, since that's how real troubleshooting actually happens on the job.

technicalQuestions.question: Can you walk me through the layers of the OSI model?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Fluency, not memorization for its own sake — troubleshooting language in this field maps directly onto these layers, so this is really checking whether that vocabulary is second nature yet.
strongAnswerCovers: All 7 layers in order, even if briefly (Physical through Application)
Where common troubleshooting maps — e.g. cabling is Layer 1, routing is Layer 3, firewalls span several
Comfort using the layer number as shorthand, like 'that's a Layer 4 problem'

technicalQuestions.question: What is a firewall, and how does it decide what traffic to allow or block?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Whether you know there are real different firewall types (packet-filtering, stateful, next-gen) rather than treating 'firewall' as one generic blocker.
strongAnswerCovers: Packet-filtering: rule-based on IP/port only, no connection awareness
Stateful: tracks connection state, understands that a reply belongs to an earlier request
Next-gen: adds application-awareness, intrusion prevention, and more

technicalQuestions.question: What's the difference between a stateful and a stateless firewall?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Understanding of connection-state tracking specifically — a very commonly asked follow-up once firewalls come up at all.
strongAnswerCovers: Stateless evaluates every packet independently against static rules
Stateful tracks the connection itself, automatically allowing return traffic for an approved outbound request
Why that matters: stateless needs explicit rules for both directions, stateful doesn't

technicalQuestions.question: How does a VPN create a secure tunnel between two points?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Baseline encryption/tunneling concepts — you don't need protocol-level depth, but you should be able to explain what's actually being protected and how.
strongAnswerCovers: Encapsulation: original traffic wrapped inside a new encrypted packet
Encryption protects confidentiality across an untrusted network (the public internet)
What's actually protected: the data in transit, not the endpoints themselves

technicalQuestions.question: What's the difference between an IDS and an IPS?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: The detect-and-alert versus detect-and-block distinction — a frequently asked pairing question, similar to the SOC track's version of the same question.
strongAnswerCovers: IDS: passive, monitors and alerts only
IPS: in-line, can actively block or drop traffic in real time
Tradeoff: an IPS can cause outages via false positives; an IDS can't stop anything by itself

technicalQuestions.question: How would you troubleshoot a firewall rule that's blocking traffic it shouldn't?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: A methodical troubleshooting process (check the specific rule, check rule order, check logs, test from the source) rather than a vague 'I'd look at the logs.'
strongAnswerCovers: Check the specific rule first — is there one that should match, and does it?
Check rule order — an earlier rule can shadow a correct one below it
Check logs for what the firewall actually did with the traffic
Test directly from the source, not just from documentation

roles.formatNote: Entry-level generalist interviews tend to sample lightly across SOC, VAPT, and network-security topics rather than going deep on one — expect a broad, mostly definitional first pass rather than heavy scenario-based questioning, and use it as a chance to signal which direction actually interests you.

technicalQuestions.question: What's the CIA triad, and why does it matter?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: The most common true-beginner framing question across the whole field — confidentiality, integrity, availability, and whether you can connect each to a real example.
strongAnswerCovers: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability — all three, not just one or two
A real example for each (encryption for confidentiality, checksums for integrity, redundancy for availability)
Why all three matter together — a system can fail by violating any one of them

technicalQuestions.question: What's the difference between a vulnerability assessment and a penetration test?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Whether you can distinguish broad automated detection from manual, goal-directed exploitation — useful even if you end up on the defensive side.
strongAnswerCovers: VA: broad, often automated scanning for known vulnerabilities
PT: manual, goal-directed exploitation of real attack paths
PT usually follows VA, digging into what's actually exploitable

technicalQuestions.question: Can you walk me through the layers of the OSI model?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Foundational networking fluency that underpins every track, from SIEM log-reading to firewall troubleshooting.
strongAnswerCovers: All 7 layers in order, even briefly
Where common troubleshooting maps onto specific layers
Comfort using layer numbers as shorthand in conversation

technicalQuestions.question: What is a firewall, and how does it filter traffic?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Whether you know there are different firewall types, not just that 'a firewall blocks bad stuff.'
strongAnswerCovers: Different firewall types exist (packet-filtering, stateful, next-gen)
Basic idea: rules decide what traffic to allow or deny based on criteria like IP, port, or connection state

technicalQuestions.question: What is SIEM, and have you had any hands-on exposure to one?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Hands-on curiosity — even brief exposure to a free trial or lab environment signals initiative here.
strongAnswerCovers: What a SIEM actually does: aggregates and correlates logs from many sources
Any hands-on exposure, even a free trial or lab — genuine curiosity matters more than deep expertise here

technicalQuestions.question: If several incidents came in at once, how would you decide what to work first?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Basic prioritization judgment — you're not expected to have a formal severity framework memorized, just a sensible reasoning process.
strongAnswerCovers: A sensible reasoning process (impact plus urgency), not a formal framework memorized
Willingness to escalate or ask rather than guessing under pressure

technicalQuestions.question: What's the difference between an IDS and an IPS?
technicalQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: The detect-and-alert versus detect-and-block distinction — a small but frequently asked check of whether terms you use are actually understood, not just recalled.
strongAnswerCovers: IDS: passive, monitors and alerts only
IPS: in-line, can actively block or drop malicious traffic in real time

behavioralQuestions.question: Describe a time you had to respond to a high-pressure situation.
behavioralQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Composure under pressure — cybersecurity roles regularly involve time-sensitive decisions, so this checks how you actually behave, not just whether you can define stress.

behavioralQuestions.question: Give an example of a time you used teamwork to accomplish something.
behavioralQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Whether you can collaborate — security work is rarely solo, especially escalations that hand off between people.

behavioralQuestions.question: Tell me about a time you had to relay bad news to someone.
behavioralQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Communication under an uncomfortable circumstance — a real skill when you're the one telling a team their system has a problem.

behavioralQuestions.question: How have you explained a technical issue to someone non-technical?
behavioralQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Whether you can translate — most of this field involves explaining risk to people who don't share your vocabulary.

behavioralQuestions.question: Have you ever handled sensitive information? How did you approach it?
behavioralQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Trustworthiness and judgment around confidentiality, even in a non-security prior role — the specific context matters less than the care you describe.

behavioralQuestions.question: Describe a time you noticed a potential risk or problem and what you did about it.
behavioralQuestions.whatTheyreChecking: Initiative — whether you act on something you notice rather than waiting to be told, which is exactly the instinct this field rewards.

behavioralFramework.name: STAR method
behavioralFramework.description: A standard, widely-taught way to structure behavioral answers: Situation (briefly set the scene), Task (what you were responsible for), Action (the specific steps you took), Result (the outcome, ideally with a concrete detail). It's not specific to cybersecurity interviews — it's general interview advice — but it's worth using deliberately for every behavioral question above rather than answering in the abstract.

workedExample.situation: During a college group project, I noticed a shared Drive folder with our team's files was set to "Anyone with the link can edit," including a file with some teammates' personal contact details.
workedExample.task: As the one who spotted it, I felt responsible for flagging it before it caused a real problem, even though permissions weren't officially anyone's assigned job.
workedExample.action: I messaged the team lead directly instead of the group chat, to avoid causing alarm, explained the specific risk in plain terms, and proposed switching the folder to restricted access with named collaborators only. Once they agreed, I helped make the change myself.
workedExample.result: The folder was locked down within the day, nothing was actually leaked, and double-checking sharing settings became the team's default habit before adding new files afterward.
